quiz.why: Measuring gives a picture at one point in time, while monitoring tracks IC regularly through indicators and targets so that management can act early. Human capital is tracked through training, staff turnover and the number of inventors. Employees are not shown as assets in the accounts.

quiz.q: A company's IC dashboard has 85 loosely defined indicators, none with a named owner or data source, chosen before its strategy was agreed. What is the best criticism?
quiz.ok: Start from strategy and use a few clear indicators, each with an owner
no: More indicators generally give a fuller and more accurate picture of IC
Named owners matter little once a dashboard is updated automatically
Indicators should be fixed first, so that the strategy can follow them
quiz.why: A monitoring system starts from strategy and selects a small number of clearly defined indicators, each with a named owner and data source, then sets targets, reports results and reviews the indicators regularly. Choosing indicators before strategy reverses the logic, because indicators exist to track the strategy.

quiz.concept: IP as an answer to the information paradox
quiz.q: An inventor wants to sell her know-how to a manufacturer, which will not pay until it has seen what it is buying. How do IP rights help resolve this problem?
quiz.ok: A patent or an NDA lets her disclose without losing protection
no: Disclosure to one buyer never reduces the value of knowledge
The buyer can pay a price fixed by the cost approach unseen
Defensive publication lets the buyer assess it without any risk
quiz.why: The information paradox is that a buyer cannot judge knowledge without seeing it, but once it is seen it has been given away. Patents and confidentiality agreements allow disclosure without loss of protection. Defensive publication would give the knowledge to everyone, destroying what she wants to sell.

quiz.q: Apprentices learn a master craftsman's technique by working beside him for months. Later the firm interviews him and writes his method down in a manual. Which SECI stages are these, in order?
quiz.ok: Socialisation, then externalisation
no: Externalisation, then combination
Internalisation, then socialisation
Combination, then internalisation
quiz.why: Socialisation passes tacit knowledge to tacit knowledge through shared experience, as with the apprentices. Externalisation turns tacit knowledge into explicit form, as with the manual. Combination joins explicit knowledge with explicit knowledge, and internalisation turns explicit knowledge back into tacit know-how.

quiz.q: A firm's process knowledge is valuable and rare, but rivals can reach the same result just as cheaply by a different route. Does it meet the VRIN test for competitive advantage?
quiz.ok: No, because the knowledge is substitutable
no: Yes, because value and rarity are enough
No, because the knowledge is tacit, not explicit
Yes, provided it is written down as explicit knowledge
quiz.why: Knowledge gives competitive advantage when it is valuable, rare, hard to imitate and not substitutable. A different route to the same result is a substitute, so the advantage will not last. Whether the knowledge is tacit or explicit is not one of the four tests.

quiz.q: A firm's engineers are unusually good at spotting the worth of research done outside the firm, by universities and suppliers, and putting it to work in the firm's own products. Which concept describes this ability?
quiz.ok: Absorptive capacity
no: Core competence
Dynamic capability
Socialisation
quiz.why: Absorptive capacity is the ability to recognise and use outside knowledge. Dynamic capabilities are the broader ability to sense opportunities, seize them and reconfigure resources, while core competencies are forms of collective learning that open many markets. Socialisation is the SECI stage of sharing tacit knowledge, not an ability to use external research.

quiz.q: A retailer's most valuable knowledge asset is a database of customer behaviour that includes personal data. It protects the database through confidentiality agreements and access controls. What further legal regime must it consider?
quiz.ok: Data protection law, which governs the personal data in the database
no: Copyright registration, which is needed before the database is protected
Design registration, which protects the structure of the database
Collective licensing of the database through a copyright society
quiz.why: Knowledge assets are protected through IP rights, trade secret policies, non-disclosure agreements and contract clauses, but knowledge that includes personal data is also subject to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Confidentiality protects the firm's interest in the data; it does not displace the separate data protection regime.

quiz.concept: IP actions at the concept stage
quiz.q: A product team has moved from raw ideas to a defined product concept. Which IP action belongs at this stage of development?
quiz.ok: Checking patentability and freedom to operate
no: Registering trade marks and doing final clearance
Binding testers by NDAs and filing improvements
Watching competitors and enforcing granted rights
quiz.why: At the concept stage, patentability and freedom to operate should be checked before money is committed to design. Trade mark registration and final clearance belong at launch, NDAs for testers belong to testing, and watching and enforcing come after launch.

quiz.q: The main patent application has been filed. During field trials, outside testers handle the prototype, and several suggest improvements. What should IP management require at this stage?
quiz.ok: NDAs binding the testers, and filings for the improvements
no: A public announcement of the improvements to fix their priority
Defensive publication of the prototype to keep the field free
Trade mark registration before the testers see the product
quiz.why: During testing, non-disclosure agreements should bind testers and improvements should be filed, because public disclosure before filing usually destroys novelty. A public announcement or defensive publication would make the improvements prior art against the firm's own later applications. A trade mark protects the brand, not the invention.

quiz.q: A pharmaceutical firm develops a new salt form of a known drug that shows no improvement in therapeutic efficacy. Which legal hurdle should shape its development plans in India?
quiz.ok: New forms of known substances need enhanced efficacy to be patentable
no: Salt forms count as new chemical entities and so are patentable in India
Medicines in India can be protected only by trade secrets, not patents
A new form is patentable if it is filed before the original patent expires
quiz.why: Indian patent law bars patents on new forms of known substances unless they show enhanced efficacy. A salt of a known drug is such a new form, not a new chemical entity, and the timing of filing does not cure the missing efficacy; medicines can still be patented when the test is met. Because this exclusion shapes pharmaceutical development, it should be checked early, when patentability is assessed. Authority: Patents Act, s. 3(d).

quiz.concept: Searching patents before entering a field
quiz.q: A firm starts heavy R&D in a technical field that is new to it, without searching the patent literature, aiming to file quickly once it has results. Which risk does the guidance to check others' patents first address?
quiz.ok: Spending on work that duplicates existing solutions or infringes others' patents
no: Destroying its own novelty by reading publicly available patent documents
Breaching a duty of confidence by studying competitors' published claims
Losing its priority date, because searching delays the filing of its application
quiz.why: The guidance is to check others' patents before entering a new field and to search patent literature at the idea stage for existing solutions. Skipping this risks spending on work that already exists or that infringes, leaving the firm without freedom to operate. Reading published patents is lawful and does not affect the firm's own novelty.

quiz.q: A firm's opening patent stock is zero. It obtains 20, 10 and 30 patents in 2023, 2024 and 2025. Using K(t) = (1 minus δ) × K(t−1) + P(t) with δ = 15 per cent, and no depreciation of each year's new patents in that year, what is the depreciated stock at the end of 2025?
quiz.why: K(2023) = 20; K(2024) = 0.85 × 20 + 10 = 27; K(2025) = 0.85 × 27 + 30 = 52.95. The simple count is 60, depreciating each year's new patents in the year they arrive gives 45.01, and multiplying the old stock by δ instead of (1 minus δ) gives 31.95.

quiz.q: A firm holds 400 patents, 60 of them in battery technology. Worldwide there are 20 lakh patents, 1 lakh of them in battery technology. What is the firm's revealed technological advantage (RTA) in batteries, and what does it show?
quiz.ok: 3.00; the firm is relatively specialised in battery technology
no: 0.33; the firm is relatively weak in battery technology
10.00; the firm's share beats the world share by ten points
0.89; the firm is slightly under-specialised in batteries
quiz.why: RTA = (60 ÷ 400) ÷ (1 lakh ÷ 20 lakh) = 0.15 ÷ 0.05 = 3.00, so the firm is specialised in batteries relative to the world. Inverting the ratio gives 0.33, subtracting the two shares gives a gap of ten points rather than a ratio, and using the shares outside batteries gives 0.89.

quiz.concept: The counting unit must be stated
quiz.q: Two reports on the same firm give its patent stock as 480 and 160. Neither says how it counted. What is the most likely explanation, and the lesson?
quiz.ok: They used different counting units, which must always be stated
no: One must be wrong, since a firm has only one true patent count
The lower figure is depreciated, so it is always the better one
The higher figure is citation weighted, so it measures quality
quiz.why: A patent stock can be counted as applications or grants, patent families, active patents, citation-weighted or quality-adjusted counts, or a depreciated stock, and these give very different numbers. Counting one invention once per country rather than once per family, for example, multiplies the figure. Granstrand insists that the counting unit must always be stated.

quiz.q: An analyst compares raw patent counts and concludes that a pharmaceutical firm is less innovative than a consumer electronics firm with five times as many patents. Which limit of patent stocks makes this comparison unsound?
quiz.ok: Industries patent at very different rates
no: Company names vary across patent records
Publication lags filing by about 18 months
Raw counts give older patents less weight
quiz.why: Industries patent at different rates, so raw counts cannot fairly compare firms in different sectors. Varying company names and the publication delay are real limits, but they affect any count and do not explain why firms in different sectors file at such different rates. Raw counts give old and new patents equal weight, which is why depreciated stocks exist.

quiz.concept: Why older patents count for less
quiz.q: Why does a depreciated patent stock give less weight to a firm's older patents than a simple count does?
quiz.ok: Knowledge becomes outdated, so older patents add less to the stock
no: Older patents have fewer claims than patents filed more recently
Older patents are usually revoked within a few years of grant
Renewal fees on older patents are lower, so they matter less
quiz.why: The depreciated stock gives less weight to older patents because knowledge becomes outdated, and δ is the yearly rate of decline. The formula turns on the ageing of knowledge, not on claims, fees or revocation, which it does not measure. That is why a firm with 106 patents over seven years can have a depreciated stock of only about 74.

quiz.q: Why do radio stations, hotels and event organisers usually take blanket licences from copyright societies rather than negotiate with each owner?
quiz.ok: Separate deals with thousands of owners would be impossibly costly
no: Individual owners are barred by law from licensing their own works
Blanket licences are cheaper because they pay nothing to authors
Societies own the copyright in every work in their repertoire
quiz.why: Users need thousands of works, and negotiating separately with every owner would be impossibly costly, while individual owners cannot monitor use across the country. A society therefore grants blanket licences covering its whole repertoire and distributes the income to members. Owners keep the right to license their own works individually.

quiz.q: A composer belongs to a registered copyright society but wants to license one of her songs directly to a film producer. Can she?
quiz.ok: Yes, as owners keep the right to license their own works individually
no: No, because joining a society transfers her licensing rights to it
No, because only a registered society may grant a licence in any work
Yes, but not until the society's five-year registration has lapsed
quiz.why: The business of issuing or granting licences may be carried on only by or through a registered copyright society, but owners keep the right to license their own works individually. The restriction is on carrying on the business of licensing, not on an owner dealing with her own work. Authority: Copyright Act, 1957, s. 33.

quiz.concept: Licensing business needs a registered society
quiz.q: An unregistered company starts the business of granting licences in music on behalf of hundreds of composers who have signed up with it. What is the legal position?
quiz.ok: That business may be carried on only by or through a registered society
no: It is lawful, because each composer has signed a contract with the company
It is lawful, provided the company publishes a tariff scheme for users
It is lawful for five years, after which the company must register
quiz.why: The business of issuing or granting licences in works may be carried on only by or through a registered copyright society. Contracts with members do not replace registration, and publishing a tariff scheme is a duty of registered societies, not a way around registration. Registration, once granted, lasts five years. Authority: Copyright Act, 1957, ss. 33 and 33A.

quiz.concept: Why the law regulates copyright societies
quiz.q: Why does copyright law require societies to publish tariff schemes, give owners control over the society and file returns and audited accounts?
quiz.ok: A dominant society in each class may set high tariffs and unfair terms
no: Societies are government departments, so they must account to Parliament
Societies compete fiercely, so their tariffs need protection from falling
Societies lack power to enforce rights, so the State enforces for them
quiz.why: Because one society tends to dominate each class of works, collective management raises concerns about high tariffs, unfair treatment of users, unclear distribution and high costs. The law responds with published tariffs, owner control and returns and audited accounts. The risk is too much power, not too little: societies are private bodies that enforce rights themselves, and they do not face fierce competition. Authority: Copyright Act, 1957, ss. 33A, 35 and 36.

quiz.q: A radio broadcaster wants to play an old song whose owner it cannot trace and who never joined any copyright society. How does its position differ in a country where collective management is extended by law, compared with one where it is purely voluntary?
quiz.ok: The society's licence can cover the song even though its owner is not a member
no: Nothing changes: it must still trace the owner and agree a separate licence
The song falls into the public domain, because its owner never joined a society
The broadcaster may play it free until the owner comes forward to claim royalties
quiz.why: Collective management may be voluntary, extended to non-members by law (as in the Nordic countries), or mandatory for certain rights. Under a purely voluntary system a society licenses its members' repertoire, so the broadcaster would have to find the owner; extension lets the society's licence reach non-members' works as well. Not joining a society does not end copyright or make use free.

quiz.concept: Other flaws in the market-book gap
quiz.q: An analyst treats the whole gap between a knowledge company's market value and its book value as the value of its intellectual capital. Apart from market mood and growth expectations, what else makes the gap a poor measure?
quiz.ok: It also reflects undervalued tangible assets and hidden liabilities
no: It is fixed at the date of the last audited balance sheet
It leaves out human capital, which only scorecards can capture
It excludes brands, which the accounts already carry at fair value
quiz.why: The residual method is unreliable because the gap includes market mood and growth expectations, ignores undervalued tangible assets and hidden liabilities, and changes every day. Internally generated brands are not in the accounts at all, so the gap already includes them, along with people and relationships. Knowledge companies are better valued from cash flows, multiples or the sum of their parts.

quiz.concept: The residual method after a price move
quiz.q: A knowledge company has a market value of ₹5,000 crore and book value of ₹1,500 crore. Next month its share price rises by 10 per cent, and its book value is unchanged. What does the residual method now show, and what does that reveal?
quiz.ok: ₹4,000 crore, though nothing changed inside: the method is unreliable
no: ₹3,850 crore, because the gap itself grows by the same ten per cent
₹3,500 crore, because the gap stays fixed until the next balance sheet
₹4,000 crore, which shows that its IC grew by ₹500 crore in a month
quiz.why: Market value rises to ₹5,500 crore, so the gap is 5,500 minus 1,500 = ₹4,000 crore, although nothing inside the firm has changed. The gap includes market mood and growth expectations and changes every day, so it is not a reliable value of intellectual capital. Growing only the gap by 10 per cent gives ₹3,850 crore, and leaving it at ₹3,500 crore ignores the price move.

quiz.q: A buyer will acquire a knowledge company outright, paying its shareholders and taking over its debt. Which measure of value captures what the buyer is acquiring?
quiz.ok: Enterprise value, the value of the business to all providers of capital
no: Equity value, the value of the whole business to its shareholders alone
IP value, the value of its legal rights and the income they protect
Asset value, the total of the values of its individual assets
quiz.why: Enterprise value is the value of the business to all providers of capital and equals equity value plus net debt, so it is the right measure when the buyer takes over the debt as well as the shares. Equity value is only the shareholders' part. IP value and asset value measure parts of the business rather than the whole.

quiz.concept: Enterprise value when cash exceeds debt
quiz.q: A knowledge company has an equity value of ₹1,200 crore, borrowings of ₹150 crore and cash of ₹350 crore. Taking net debt as borrowings less cash, what is its enterprise value?
quiz.ok: ₹1,000 crore
no: ₹1,400 crore
₹1,350 crore
₹1,200 crore
quiz.why: Net debt is 150 minus 350 = minus ₹200 crore, so enterprise value = equity value plus net debt = 1,200 minus 200 = ₹1,000 crore. Adding the cash surplus instead gives ₹1,400 crore, adding gross borrowings gives ₹1,350 crore, and ignoring net debt leaves the equity value of ₹1,200 crore.

quiz.q: A pharmaceutical knowledge company has a pipeline of early drug candidates, each of which may be dropped or advanced as trial results come in. Which valuation method best suits the pipeline?
quiz.ok: Real options, valuing the flexibility to advance or drop each candidate
no: The residual method, which treats market minus book value as its value
Historical cost, which records the R&D actually spent on each candidate
Customer lifetime value, which values its existing base of customers
quiz.why: Knowledge companies are valued by discounted cash flow with scenarios, market multiples, adding up the parts, real options for research pipelines and customer lifetime value. A pipeline's value lies in the right to continue or stop at each stage, which option models capture. The residual method is unreliable, and historical cost is not value.

quiz.concept: Treating R&D as investment in valuation
quiz.q: When valuing a knowledge company, why might an analyst first treat its R&D spending as an investment rather than as an expense?
quiz.ok: Expensing R&D hides the investment that drives the firm's future value
no: Accounting rules already require all R&D to be recorded as an asset
Treating R&D as investment raises the deductions the firm can claim
Doing so removes the need to forecast the firm's future cash flows
quiz.why: Under Ind AS 38 research is always expensed and development is recognised only when six conditions are met, so the accounts understate the investment that builds a knowledge company's value. Analysts sometimes treat R&D as an investment to correct this before applying discounted cash flow or multiples. It changes the analysis, not the accounts or the tax position.

quiz.q: A university lab builds a working prototype of a low-cost water filter and obtains a patent on it. Five years later, no filter has been sold to anyone. In the notes' terms, what has happened so far?
quiz.ok: An invention has been made, but no innovation yet, since nothing has reached the market
no: An innovation has occurred, since the patent grant shows the idea is new and useful
Diffusion has begun, since publication of the patent spreads the idea through the field
An incremental innovation has occurred, since the filter improves on earlier filters
quiz.why: An invention is a new idea or device, innovation is its successful introduction into the market, and diffusion is its spread among users. A patent protects the invention but does not commercialise it, so neither innovation nor diffusion has happened. Publication spreads information, not use, which is why the diffusion option fails.

quiz.q: Using the classification of innovation by architecture, a firm keeps every core component technology of its product exactly as before but redesigns how those components are linked and interact. How is this change classified?
quiz.ok: Architectural innovation, since the core ideas are kept while the links between them change
no: Modular innovation, since the components are rearranged while their designs stay the same
Radical innovation, since the product as a whole now works in a different way
Incremental innovation, since none of the core component technologies has been replaced
quiz.why: On the architecture dimension, incremental innovation leaves both core ideas and links unchanged, modular innovation replaces core ideas but keeps the links, architectural innovation keeps core ideas but changes the links, and radical innovation changes both. Here only the links change, so the change is architectural. The modular option reverses the definition, since modular means new components in an old configuration.

quiz.q: An IP manager proposes filing patents in every field the R&D lab touches, before the board has decided which markets the company will enter. What does the 'strategy ladder' suggest is wrong with this?
quiz.ok: IP choices should follow the business and innovation strategy rather than lead it
no: IP strategy sits at the top of the ladder, so it should set the business direction
Filing should wait until the product is launched and its sales are known
The ladder puts IP level with business strategy, so neither should follow the other
quiz.why: The strategy ladder places IP strategy below the firm's business, innovation, technology and commercialisation strategies, so IP choices should follow business choices. Filing in every field spends money on rights that may serve no chosen market. Waiting until launch is a different error, because filing must come before disclosure and early filing matters most for radical innovation.

quiz.q: In an electric-scooter market, many rival layouts competed for some years. Most makers have now converged on one layout, and competition is mainly about price and manufacturing methods. What best explains this stage?
quiz.ok: A dominant design has emerged, so competition shifts to price and process
no: The technology is at the start of its S curve, where performance rises fastest
A disruptive innovation is complete, since mainstream customers now buy scooters
Network effects have taken over, so the common layout earns royalties from all makers
quiz.why: Markets often settle on a dominant design, after which competition shifts to price and process, which fits the convergence described. The S-curve option is wrong twice over: improvement is slow at the start of the curve, and convergence signals maturity rather than a beginning. Royalties from all implementers arise from patents included in standards, not from a common layout as such.

quiz.q: A hospital chain finds that its doctors need a cheaper portable heart monitor and asks a device maker to build one. Separately, a university lab discovers a new graphene sensor and then looks for products that could use it. How are these sources of innovation classified?
quiz.ok: The heart monitor is market pull; the graphene sensor is technology push
no: The heart monitor is technology push; the graphene sensor is market pull
Both are technology push, since each produces a new piece of hardware
Both are market pull, since each will in the end be sold to customers
quiz.why: Technology push occurs when new science creates products, and market pull occurs when customer needs drive development. The monitor starts from doctors' needs, while the sensor starts from a discovery in search of uses. That every innovation ends up in a market, or involves hardware, does not decide its source; what matters is where development began.

quiz.q: A firm's smart glasses have so far been bought only by innovators and early adopters. Under Rogers' account of diffusion, which group must the firm win next, and why does that group matter?
quiz.ok: The early majority, the next group in sequence, with whom adoption reaches the mainstream
no: The laggards, since the most reluctant buyers must be won before the mainstream follows
The late majority, since cautious buyers adopt directly after the early adopters
No further group, since diffusion is complete once the early adopters have bought
quiz.why: Rogers' adopter groups follow in order: innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards. Innovators and early adopters are only about one-sixth of users, while the early and late majorities together are about two-thirds, so the early majority is the next and decisive group. The late majority follows the early majority, and laggards come last.

quiz.concept: IP plan for a radical breakthrough
quiz.q: A start-up has invented a battery chemistry that doubles energy density and could create an entirely new market. Which IP plan best fits the notes' advice for radical innovation?
quiz.ok: File early with broad claims, then quickly file follow-up patents around it
no: Delay filing until the product is commercially proven, then file narrow claims covering it
Rely mainly on speed and the business model, since patents add little value here
File only narrow claims, so that the patent can never be opposed or revoked
quiz.why: A radical innovator should file early with broad claims, seek strategic patents that rivals cannot easily invent around and quickly file follow-up patents, because a second race for surrounding patents follows a key patent. Relying on speed and the business model is the disrupter's strategy. Narrow claims give away the breadth that makes a pioneer patent strategic; the answer to opposition risk is drafting that withstands the inventive step test.

quiz.q: After a pioneer obtains a key patent on a radical technology, rivals start filing many patents on improvements and applications around it. Why should the pioneer worry?
quiz.ok: Rivals' surrounding patents can hem in its key patent and give them bargaining power
no: Later improvement patents shorten the remaining term of the pioneer's key patent
Rivals' later filings become prior art that can then be used to revoke the pioneer's key patent
Surrounding patents give their owners a share in the ownership of the key patent
quiz.why: A key patent sets off a second race for surrounding patents, and if rivals win it they hold the improvements and applications the pioneer needs and can use them as bargaining chips. That is why the pioneer should file follow-up patents quickly. Later filings cannot be prior art against an earlier patent, and they neither shorten its term nor give their owners a share in it.

quiz.q: A bank offers a short-term loan, with repayments starting after six months, to fund a radical biotech platform that may take years to reach the market. Why is this a poor fit?
quiz.ok: Radical projects take long and are uncertain, so they need patient finance
no: Indian law does not allow loans to be secured on patents or other IP rights
Radical projects carry little risk, so the loan's interest rate is simply too high
Radical patents earn royalties at once, so selling future royalties would suit it better
quiz.why: Radical innovation involves high uncertainty and cost and long development, so it needs patient finance such as venture capital, government grants or staged corporate investment. Repayments starting after six months demand cash long before the project can earn any. IP-backed lending is lawful in India, radical projects are high in risk rather than low, and a platform still years from market has no royalty stream to sell.

quiz.concept: Complementary assets risk in radical innovation
quiz.q: A two-person start-up has a working, patented prototype of a radically better imaging scanner, and hospitals are keen to buy it. It has no factory, no sales network and no service engineers. Which risk of radical innovation does this most directly show?
quiz.ok: Lack of the complementary assets needed to make, sell and support the product
no: Technical failure, since a radical technology may never work as intended
Slow adoption, since customers hesitate to buy unfamiliar technologies
Weak IP, since a start-up cannot obtain strategic patents on its own
quiz.why: Radical projects face risks of technical failure, slow adoption, lack of complementary assets and regulatory delay. Here the prototype works and buyers are keen, so the gap lies in the manufacturing, sales and service capacity needed to commercialise it, which are complementary assets. A start-up can hold strategic patents as well as any firm, so weak IP is not the problem shown.

quiz.q: A start-up sells a basic, cheap ultrasound device with poorer images than hospital machines. Its first buyers are rural clinics that had never owned any ultrasound equipment. Over time it improves and begins selling to city hospitals. How is this best classified?
quiz.ok: New-market disruption, since it began with non-consumers and a good-enough product
no: Low-end disruption, since it began with the leaders' least profitable existing customers
Radical innovation, since it created an entirely new technology base for imaging
Sustaining innovation, since it improved until mainstream hospitals were willing to buy it
quiz.why: A disrupter starts either at the low end, serving customers the leaders neglect, or in a new market, serving people who were not buying at all. Rural clinics that never owned ultrasound are non-consumers, so this is new-market disruption, completed as mainstream customers adopt it. Low-end disruption would require the first buyers to be existing customers whom the leaders were neglecting.

quiz.concept: Better main-market entry is not disruption
quiz.q: A ride-hailing app entered the main market with a service that mainstream customers found better than taxis from the start, and it grew rapidly. A commentator calls it a textbook disruption because it hurt incumbents. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
quiz.ok: Disrupters start at the low end or in new markets, not in the main market
no: Disruption requires patented technology, and the app's advantage was never patented
Disruption requires an entrant with more resources than the established firms it challenges
Disruption is complete only when every incumbent firm has left the market
quiz.why: Disruption is a process in which a smaller firm starts at the low end or in a new market with a good-enough offering and then moves up. A firm that begins in the main market with a better service is not disruptive in this sense, which is why the app is said not to be a disrupter. Hurting incumbents is not the test, and disruption is complete when mainstream customers adopt the product, not when every incumbent leaves.

quiz.q: Which statement best distinguishes disruptive innovation from radical innovation?
quiz.ok: Disruption turns on a cheap, good-enough entry; radical on a major technical leap
no: Disruptive products outperform incumbents' products at launch; radical products start out cheaper
Radical innovation comes only from entrants; disruption comes only from established firms
They are one idea, described once from the inventor's side and once from the market's
quiz.why: Radical innovation is a major technical change that creates a new technology base, a large jump in performance or a new market. Disruption is a market process in which a simpler, cheaper, good-enough product, usually worse at first on conventional measures, lets a smaller firm displace leaders. Disruption should therefore not be confused with technical novelty, and the claim that disruptive products outperform at launch reverses the usual pattern.

quiz.q: An Indian start-up is disrupting a market with a new subscription business model delivered through its own app. Which protection mix fits the notes best?
quiz.ok: Software copyright, trade secrets, brands and contracts, as business methods as such are unpatentable
no: A patent on the subscription business method itself, since the model is the start-up's real advantage
Broad pioneer patents on the model, followed by surrounding patents to block followers
No legal protection at all, since disrupters rely only on speed and network effects
quiz.why: Disrupters rely more on business models, speed and network effects than on patents, and business methods as such are not patentable in India. Their protection therefore comes mainly from copyright in software, trade secrets, brands and contracts. Relying more on speed does not mean relying on nothing, which is why the no-protection option fails. Authority: s. 3(k), Patents Act.

quiz.q: An incumbent with a large patent portfolio built for sustaining innovation sees a low-end entrant succeeding with a new business model. What does the notes' analysis advise?
quiz.ok: Watch such entrants, create a separate unit, or invest in or acquire the newcomer
no: Sue the entrant, since a large sustaining portfolio will reliably block a new business model
Ignore the entrant, since low-margin customers never affect the leaders' main market
File more follow-up patents on existing products, which will keep the entrant out
quiz.why: Portfolios built for sustaining innovation may not block a new business model, so litigation or more follow-up patents are unlikely to stop the entrant. Disrupters improve and move into the main market, so ignoring them is dangerous. The advice is to watch low-end and new-market entrants, create separate units, or invest in or acquire the newcomers.

quiz.q: A carmaker launches a faster, more comfortable version of its best-selling sedan for its existing customers. Separately, it rebuilds its paint shop to cut toxic emissions. Reading 'sustaining' in the market-effect sense, how are the two projects best classified?
quiz.ok: The sedan is sustaining innovation; the paint shop is sustainable (green) innovation
no: The sedan is disruptive innovation; the paint shop is sustainable (green) innovation
Both are sustaining innovation, since each improves the firm's existing business
Both are sustainable innovation, since each helps the firm's business endure
quiz.why: Sustaining innovation improves existing products for existing customers, which is what the new sedan does, while sustainable (green) innovation reduces environmental harm, as the cleaner paint shop does. The two terms name different ideas, which is why an answer should say which meaning it uses. The sedan is not disruptive, because disruption starts with a cheaper, good-enough product at the low end or in a new market, not a better product for current customers.

quiz.q: Why do established firms usually win contests over sustaining innovation?
quiz.ok: They have the resources and motivation to improve products for existing customers
no: Sustaining innovations are small steps, so entrants have little to gain from them
Patent law gives existing firms a priority right over improvements to their products
Sustaining innovations target non-consumers, whom large firms reach more easily
quiz.why: Sustaining innovation improves existing products for existing customers, by small steps or major breakthroughs, and established firms have both the resources and the motivation to win these contests. That is why the matching IP strategy is continuous follow-up patenting, large portfolios and cross-licensing. Serving non-consumers is the mark of new-market disruption, not of sustaining innovation.

quiz.q: A firm holds patents on a low-emission cement process. It wants the process widely adopted in developing countries while still earning from it. Which approach fits the notes' account of sustainable innovation?
quiz.ok: License widely, use platforms linking owners and users, and transfer through partnerships
no: License the patents but withhold the know-how, so that partners stay dependent
License one partner exclusively, since exclusivity is what makes green patents attract investment
Dedicate the patents to the public, since free use is the only way green technology spreads
quiz.why: For green innovation the IP questions concern diffusion: green patents attract investment, wide licensing can spread clean technology, platforms such as WIPO GREEN connect owners and users, and transfer to developing countries takes place through licences and partnerships. Keeping the patents and licensing them widely lets the firm earn while the technology spreads. Withholding know-how or licensing a single partner exclusively slows that diffusion, and dedicating the patents to the public gives up the earnings the firm wants.

quiz.q: A market-leading printer maker improves its flagship models every year for its existing business customers and expects its rivals to try the same. Which IP strategy matches this kind of innovation?
quiz.ok: Continuous follow-up patents, a large portfolio, cross-licensing and design and brand protection
no: Reliance on business model and speed, since patents add little to improvements
One broad pioneer patent with no follow-up, since the base technology is old
Wide licensing to all comers, since spreading the technology is the main aim
quiz.why: Sustaining innovation improves existing products for existing customers, and the matching IP strategy is continuous follow-up patenting, large portfolios, cross-licensing and protection of designs and brands. Reliance on business model and speed is the disrupter's approach, and broad pioneer patents belong to radical innovation. Wide licensing to spread a technology is a question for green innovation, not for a leader defending its position.

quiz.q: An engineer says the firm's many minor improvement patents are 'junk' and should all be dropped to save renewal fees. What is the best response under the notes?
quiz.ok: Minor patents can still be useful bargaining chips, though too many weak ones waste money
no: Drop them all, since only patents on major inventions can be enforced against rivals
Keep them all, since portfolio size is what gives a firm its bargaining power
Convert them into utility models, which are cheaper to maintain in India
quiz.why: Minor patents that engineers dismiss as 'petty' or 'junk' can still be valuable as bargaining chips, but too many weak patents waste money, so the right course is a selective review rather than wholesale dropping or keeping. A valid minor patent is as enforceable as any other, and size alone does not give value. India has no utility model or petty patent system, so conversion is not an option.

quiz.q: A drug company applies for a patent on a new crystalline form of its own known drug. It has no data showing that the new form works better therapeutically. Why is the application likely to fail, and what policy does that serve?
quiz.ok: A new form of a known substance needs enhanced efficacy, which guards against evergreening
no: Crystalline forms can be protected in India only as registered designs, not patents
A firm that already owns a patent on the drug is barred from patenting later forms of it
India grants only petty patents for such minor changes, to keep protection short
quiz.why: Indian law requires enhanced efficacy before a new form of a known substance can be patented, and obvious changes also fail the inventive step test. The purpose is to stop evergreening, the extension of protection through minor changes. India has no petty patent system, and an existing patentee is not barred from patenting genuine improvements. Authority: s. 3(d), Patents Act.

quiz.q: A consumer-appliance firm makes steady small improvements: new looks for its products each year, small functional gains and quiet improvements to its factory processes. Which protection pattern matches the notes' account of incremental innovation?
quiz.ok: Continuous patents for function, design registration for looks, secrecy for processes
no: Broad pioneer patents for function, trade marks for looks, patents for processes
Utility models for function, design registration for looks, secrecy for processes
Trade secrets for function, copyright for looks, broad patents for processes
quiz.why: Firms protect incremental innovation through continuous patenting throughout the product life, register designs for changes in appearance and keep process improvements secret. Broad pioneer patents belong to radical innovation, and India has no utility model or petty patent system. Functional gains are visible in the product once it is sold, so secrecy suits factory processes rather than product features.

quiz.concept: Matching IP emphasis to innovation degree
quiz.q: A company runs two projects. Project 1 trims cost and adds small features to its existing washing machine every year. Project 2 develops a new technology base that could create an entirely new market. Which IP emphasis fits each?
quiz.ok: Project 1: continuous patents, designs and secrets; Project 2: pioneer and strategic patents
no: Project 1: pioneer and strategic patents; Project 2: continuous patents, designs and secrets
Project 1: business model and speed; Project 2: continuous patents, designs and secrets
Project 1: utility models for each change; Project 2: pioneer and strategic patents
quiz.why: Incremental innovation makes small gains and relies on continuous patents, designs and secrets, while radical innovation creates a new technology base and calls for pioneer and strategic patents. The reversed pairing is the tempting error. Business model and speed are the disrupter's tools, and India has no utility model system for small improvements.

quiz.q: A pharmaceutical company in-licenses a molecule from a university, acquires a small start-up for its platform and runs a public contest for new formulation ideas. Which open innovation model is it using?
quiz.ok: Inbound, bringing external knowledge into the firm
no: Outbound, taking internal ideas out of the firm
Coupled, creating knowledge jointly with partners
Closed, inventing and developing everything itself
quiz.why: In the inbound or outside-in model, a firm brings in external knowledge through licensing in, acquiring start-ups, crowdsourcing and working with suppliers and users, and all three activities here import outside knowledge. Outbound would take the firm's own ideas out through licensing, sale of IP or spin-offs. Coupled would involve creating knowledge jointly with partners.

quiz.q: A firm licenses its unused sensor patents to a maker in another field and spins off a team to build a product outside its core business. Separately, it joins a consortium with rivals to develop a common standard together. Which classification is correct?
quiz.ok: The licensing and spin-off are outbound; the consortium is coupled
no: The licensing and spin-off are inbound; the consortium is outbound
The licensing is coupled; the spin-off and the consortium are outbound
All three are coupled, since each involves at least one outside party
quiz.why: Outbound or inside-out innovation takes internal ideas out through licensing, sale of IP and spin-offs. The coupled model creates knowledge jointly with partners through alliances, consortia and joint development. Involving an outside party is not enough to make an activity coupled; the test is whether knowledge is created jointly.

quiz.q: A CEO says: 'We must invent and develop everything ourselves, be first to market, and make sure nobody else ever profits from our IP.' Which open innovation assumption most directly challenges this?
quiz.ok: A better business model beats being first, and others' use of our IP can earn income
no: Openness means giving our IP away freely, so we should stop seeking to profit from it
We should close our own R&D and rely wholly on ideas from outside the firm
We should stop patenting altogether, since patents only block collaboration with outside partners
quiz.why: The CEO states the closed innovation assumptions: invent, develop and sell everything in house, be first to market, and control IP so that nobody else profits. Open innovation assumes instead that a better business model matters more than being first and that a firm should earn from others' use of its IP and buy others' IP when it helps. It uses outside ideas as well as internal ones, not instead of them, and it relies on IP rather than abandoning it, because clear ownership is what lets firms share safely.

quiz.q: After acquiring a start-up for its technology, a firm finds that its own engineers refuse to use the start-up's designs and insist on rebuilding them in house. Which drawback of open innovation does this illustrate?
quiz.ok: The 'not invented here' attitude
no: Leakage of knowledge to rivals
Disputes over ownership of new IP
Loss of control over the firm's own IP
quiz.why: Open innovation brings more ideas and faster launch but also loss of control, leakage of knowledge, the 'not invented here' attitude, coordination costs and ownership disputes. Engineers who reject outside designs simply because they come from outside show the 'not invented here' attitude. Nothing in the facts suggests knowledge leaking out or a dispute about who owns the designs.

quiz.q: During a two-year joint project with a university, a company's own lab, working separately and with its own funds, develops a related coating in parallel. After the project ends, the university develops an improvement to the project's results. How are these classified?
quiz.ok: The coating is sideground IP; the later improvement is postground IP
no: The coating is foreground IP; the later improvement is background IP
The coating is background IP; the later improvement is foreground IP
Both are foreground IP, since both relate to the project's subject matter
quiz.why: Background IP is what each party brings in, foreground IP is created in the project, sideground IP is developed in house in parallel with the project and postground IP is developed after it ends. The coating was made in parallel but outside the project, and the improvement came after it, so neither is foreground. The collaboration agreement should settle access to each category, because disputes arise at exactly these boundaries.

quiz.q: A manager argues that open innovation and IP are incompatible, because collaboration needs sharing while IP means exclusion. What is the best rebuttal under the notes?
quiz.ok: Clear ownership lets firms disclose safely and license on agreed terms
no: IP rights lapse once knowledge is shared, so the conflict disappears in practice
Open innovation uses only unprotected knowledge, so IP has no place in it
Collaboration agreements replace IP, so ownership no longer needs to be settled
quiz.why: The conflict is only apparent: firms must share to collaborate but protect to profit, and IP reconciles the two. Clear ownership lets a firm disclose knowledge safely and license it on agreed terms. That is why collaboration agreements must settle background and foreground IP rather than sidestep ownership.

quiz.q: A licensor wants to keep using its patented process in its own factory, and also promises the licensee that nobody else will be licensed. Which licence fits?
quiz.ok: A sole licence, leaving the licensor and licensee as the only users
no: An exclusive licence, which still lets the licensor use the process itself
A non-exclusive licence, which lets just one licensee use the process
A blanket licence, which bars the licensor from licensing anyone else
quiz.why: An exclusive licence excludes even the licensor, a sole licence allows only the licensor and the licensee to use the IP, and a non-exclusive licence allows many licensees. The licensor here wants to keep using the process while shutting out others, which is a sole licence. The exclusive option is the common misconception, because exclusivity would bar the licensor too.

quiz.q: A university and a company are negotiating a joint research agreement. The professor's team needs to publish its findings, while the company fears that early publication will destroy the novelty of any patent. Which part of the collaboration agreement must resolve this tension?
quiz.ok: Publication rights, setting when and how results may be published
no: Background IP, setting what each party brings into the project
A grant-back, making the university assign improvements to the company
Dispute resolution, since the tension can be settled only once it arises
quiz.why: A collaboration agreement must settle, among other things, confidentiality and publication rights, which the notes single out as important for universities. Publication before filing can destroy novelty, so the clause fixes when and how results may be published. Background IP concerns what each party brings in, a grant-back deals with improvements, and leaving the issue to dispute resolution invites the very conflict the agreement should prevent.

quiz.q: A software firm wants to put modified open source code into a closed, proprietary product that it will sell. Which licence on the borrowed code creates a problem, and why?
quiz.ok: A copyleft licence, since it requires modified versions to remain open
no: A permissive licence, since it bars use of the code in closed products
Any open source licence, since all of them forbid commercial sale
Neither kind, since open source code is free of all copyright conditions
quiz.why: Permissive licences such as MIT, BSD and Apache allow use in closed products, while copyleft licences such as the GPL require modified versions to remain open. A firm that modifies copyleft code for a closed product risks breaching the licence, which is why firms must track the open source code they use. Open source code is still licensed copyright, not free of conditions.

quiz.q: A draft patent licence requires the licensee to assign all its improvements exclusively to the licensor, never to challenge the patent's validity, and to buy unpatented raw materials only from the licensor. What is the effect under the notes?
quiz.ok: These restrictive conditions are void, so the clauses should be removed or redrafted
no: They are valid, provided the licence is in writing and registered at the patent office
They are valid, because competition law protects any condition found in an IP licence
Only the purchase condition is void; exclusive grant-backs and no-challenge terms are fine
quiz.why: Certain restrictive conditions in patent licences are void, including tying arrangements, exclusive grant-backs, bars on challenging validity and coercive package licensing. Writing and registration are separate formalities and do not cure them. Competition law protects only reasonable conditions needed to protect IP rights. Authority: s. 140, Patents Act; s. 3(5)(i), Competition Act, 2002.

quiz.concept: Choosing a freedom to operate search
quiz.q: Before launching a new e-bike motor in India, a company wants to know whether selling it would infringe any live patents. Which search should it commission?
quiz.ok: A freedom to operate search
no: A novelty or patentability search
A validity search on its own patents
A landscape search of the whole field
quiz.why: A freedom to operate search asks whether a product infringes live patents. A novelty search asks whether the firm's own invention can be patented, which is a different question, because a product can be novel and still infringe someone else's patent. A validity search asks whether a patent can be revoked, and a landscape search shows who is active in a field.

quiz.q: A firm wants to see which companies are active in solid-state battery research, how activity is trending and where the gaps are, before deciding where to invest. What should it use?
quiz.ok: A landscape search, turned into a patent map of owners, trends and gaps
no: A freedom to operate search, listing the live patents its products would infringe
A validity search, testing whether rivals' patents in the field could be revoked
A due diligence search, checking ownership, status and risk for a transaction
quiz.why: A landscape search shows who is active in a field, and patent mapping turns the results into charts of technologies, owners, trends and gaps, which is what a strategic investment decision needs. Freedom to operate, validity and due diligence searches each answer a narrower question tied to a product, a patent or a deal.

quiz.q: In March 2026 an analyst searches the databases and finds no patent applications by a rival on a technology the rival announced in October 2025. Why is it unsafe to conclude that the rival has not filed?
quiz.ok: Applications are published only after a delay, so recent filings may not show yet
no: Databases list only granted patents and never include pending applications
A rival's filings stay confidential until the patent is granted or expires
Only the official register of the rival's home country shows its filings
quiz.why: Patent applications are published only some time after filing, so an application made a few months earlier will not yet appear in any database. Databases do contain published applications, and publication does not wait for grant. Search results must therefore be read with their dates in mind, alongside other limits such as varying company names and outdated legal status.

quiz.q: A commercial database shows a competitor's Indian patent as 'in force', and its abstract seems to cover the firm's product. Before giving a freedom to operate view, what should the IP manager do?
quiz.ok: Confirm status on the official register and read the claims, which set the legal scope
no: Rely on the database, since commercial status data is updated in real time
Rely on the abstract, since it is the part that defines the scope of protection
Count the competitor's patents, since a large count shows that this one is strong
quiz.why: Legal status data in databases may be outdated, so status should always be confirmed on the official register. The claims, not the abstract, define the legal scope of a patent, so an infringement view depends on reading them. Raw counts can mislead and say nothing about whether a particular patent covers the product.

quiz.concept: Patent family data shows foreign protection
quiz.q: An IP manager finds a competitor's Indian patent on a coating and wants to know whether the same invention is also protected in Europe and the United States. Which part of the patent record should she check first?
quiz.ok: The family information, which links filings for the same invention in other countries
no: The claims, which state the countries in which the protection applies
The citations, which list the countries whose offices examined the invention
The abstract, which summarises where and how the invention is protected
quiz.why: A patent document contains bibliographic data, an abstract, a description, claims, citations, family information and legal status. Family information links the filings for the same invention in different countries, so it shows where else protection was sought, though status in each country should then be confirmed on the official register. The claims define the legal scope of protection, not its territory, and citations point to related documents rather than countries.

quiz.concept: Owning a valid patent is not freedom to operate
quiz.q: A target owns a valid Indian patent on its flagship device, and the buyer's team concludes that the target is therefore free to make and sell the device. What is wrong with this conclusion?
quiz.ok: A patent lets its owner exclude others, but the device may still infringe others' patents
no: Nothing, since a patent owner is always free to exploit its own patented invention
Validity can be confirmed only by a court, so the patent must be treated as invalid
Freedom to operate matters only once the target's own patents have expired
quiz.why: Due diligence asks four separate questions: whether the target owns or controls the IP, whether it is valid and enforceable, whether the business is free to operate without infringing others' rights, and what the IP is worth after risks. A patent gives a right to exclude others, not a right to use, so a device can be covered by its owner's valid patent and still infringe a rival's earlier patent. That is why freedom to operate is checked separately, for the particular product.

quiz.q: A target's main revenue comes from an in-licence that ends if the target undergoes a change of control. The buyer plans to acquire all of the target's shares. What should due diligence flag?
quiz.ok: The share purchase may end the licence, so consent or deal protection is needed first
no: Nothing, since buying shares never affects the contracts of the target company
The licence passes to the buyer automatically, as the new owner of the target's IP
The clause is void, as a restrictive condition prohibited in patent licences
quiz.why: Due diligence reviews licences given and taken, especially exclusivity and change of control clauses, and checks dependence on one licence. A share purchase is exactly the event such a clause targets, so the buyer must obtain the licensor's consent or protect itself through conditions, warranties or price. Change of control clauses are not among the restrictive conditions made void in patent licences.

quiz.q: An inventor orally agreed to assign his patent to Company A, which never recorded the transfer. A later sold the patent to the target by a signed, registered deed. What does a chain-of-title review conclude?
quiz.ok: The first link lacks a written, registered assignment, so the target's title is doubtful
no: Title is sound, since only the final transfer in the chain needs to be written and registered
Title is sound, since an inventor's agreement need not be recorded if he was paid
The target owns the patent but must share its profits with the original inventor
quiz.why: Chain of title requires written and registered assignments from inventors and earlier owners, not just the last transfer. If the inventor never validly assigned to Company A, A had nothing good to pass on, so the target's title is doubtful. Due diligence should require the missing assignment to be executed and registered, often as a condition before completion. Authority: ss. 68 and 69, Patents Act.

quiz.q: Due diligence finds a pending infringement suit against the target whose outcome is uncertain. How are such findings typically reflected in the deal?
quiz.ok: Through price cuts, indemnities, warranties, escrow or conditions before completion
no: By abandoning the deal, since any pending dispute makes the IP worthless
By ignoring it, since disputes are reflected only in the valuation report
By registering the transfer at once, since registration brings the pending suit to an end
quiz.why: Due diligence ends in a risk report, and its findings are reflected in the deal through price adjustment, warranties, indemnities, conditions to be met before completion and escrow. A pending suit is a risk to price and allocate, not automatically a reason to walk away. Transfers are registered after completion, and registration does nothing to a pending dispute.

quiz.q: A search of charge records shows that the target's patents are subject to a bank's security interest registered with CERSAI and the Registrar of Companies. What does this mean for the buyer?
quiz.ok: The patents are encumbered, so the charge must be cleared or priced in the deal
no: The patents are invalid until the loan is repaid, so they cannot be enforced
Nothing, since a security interest ends automatically when the IP is sold
The bank has become a joint owner, so its consent is needed before they can be licensed
quiz.why: Due diligence searches official registers and charge records for encumbrances such as charges registered with the Registrar of Companies and security interests filed with CERSAI. A charge does not affect validity or make the bank an owner, but it gives the lender rights over the asset that a buyer must clear or price. That is why encumbrances are dealt with through release, conditions before completion or price.

quiz.q: A university wants to keep owning its patent while letting a company manufacture under it in return for royalties. Which instrument fits, and why?
quiz.ok: A licence, because it permits use while ownership stays with the university
no: An assignment, because it lets the company use the patent while paying royalties
An assignment, because royalties can be paid only where ownership passes
A licence, because it transfers ownership to the company for the agreed term
quiz.why: A licence is permission to do acts that would otherwise infringe the owner's IP, and ownership remains with the licensor, whereas an assignment transfers ownership. Royalties are common in licences, so payment does not imply transfer. A licence never transfers ownership, even for a limited term.

quiz.q: A licensor is asked to grant an exclusive licence for India to a licensee who will pay only a running royalty on its sales. What risk should the drafter address, and how?
quiz.ok: The licensee may under-exploit it, so exclusivity is paired with a minimum royalty
no: Exclusivity breaches competition law, so the grant should be made non-exclusive
Exclusivity transfers ownership, so the deal should be recorded as an assignment
Running royalties cannot apply to exclusive licences, so a lump sum is required
quiz.why: Under an exclusive licence the licensor depends entirely on the licensee's sales, so a licensee who does little leaves the licensor with almost nothing. Exclusivity is therefore usually paired with a minimum royalty, an example of clauses working together. Competition law protects reasonable conditions needed to protect IP, an exclusive licence still leaves ownership with the licensor, and running royalties are common in exclusive licences.

quiz.concept: Why trade mark licences need quality control
quiz.q: Why must a trade mark licence preserve the licensor's control over the quality of the licensee's goods?
quiz.ok: So that the mark continues to indicate a single trade source to consumers
no: So that the licensor can justify a higher royalty for a premium brand
So that the licence satisfies the writing rule that applies to IP licences
So that the licensee is barred from later challenging the mark's validity
quiz.why: A trade mark tells consumers that goods come from a single trade source. If licensees could sell goods of any quality under the mark, it would stop indicating one source, so the licensor must keep control over quality. Royalty levels, writing formalities and no-challenge terms have nothing to do with this purpose.

quiz.q: A licensee insists that the licensor warrant in the licence that the licensed patent is valid. What is the usual drafting position?
quiz.ok: Warrant title but not validity, and allocate other risks by indemnities
no: Warrant title and validity, since a granted patent is beyond any challenge
Warrant nothing, since warranties have no effect in a registered licence
Warrant validity but not title, since title is shown on the register
quiz.why: Licences usually contain warranties on title, but validity is usually not warranted, because a granted patent can still be revoked, for example on prior art. Remaining risks are handled through indemnities and rules on who sues infringers and who defends claims. Warranties and indemnities must be read together.

quiz.concept: Termination must address sublicences and stock
quiz.q: A licence allows the licensee to grant sublicences, but its termination clause says only that 'on termination the licensee shall stop using the patent'. What is the main gap?
quiz.ok: It ignores existing sublicences, unsold stock and the return of materials
no: None, since sublicences always survive automatically when the head licence ends
It should also require the licensee to assign all its improvements to the licensor
It is void, since a licence that permits sublicensing cannot be terminated
quiz.why: The consequences of termination include stopping use, selling off stock, returning materials and dealing with sublicences. Because the clauses work together, a licence that permits sublicensing must say what happens to the sublicences when it ends, and silence invites disputes with sublicensees and over stock already made. Sublicences do not survive automatically, and forcing the licensee to assign its improvements would be an exclusive grant-back, which licences should avoid.

quiz.concept: What a copyright licence must identify
quiz.q: A software developer grants a company a written copyright licence that names the program and the royalty but says nothing about which rights are licensed, for how long or where. What drafting problem does this create?
quiz.ok: The licence should also identify the rights, the duration and the territory
no: None, since a copyright licence needs only to be in writing and signed
It must be registered with the Copyright Office before it can take effect
It should be an assignment instead, since software cannot be licensed
quiz.why: A copyright licence must be in writing, and because the requirements for assignments also apply to licences, it should identify the work, the rights, the duration, the territory and the royalty. A licence that is silent on the rights, term and territory invites disputes about what was granted. Copyright licences need writing, not registration, and software can be licensed like any other copyright work. Authority: ss. 30 and 30A, Copyright Act.

quiz.concept: Royalty structure for an uncertain, staged project
quiz.q: A university licenses an early-stage drug candidate to a pharmaceutical company. Nobody knows whether it will pass its trials, and the company will not pay a large sum before results are known. Which payment structure fits best?
quiz.ok: A modest upfront fee, milestone payments at each trial stage, then a running royalty
no: A large lump sum at signing, so that the university is paid whatever the trials show
A high minimum annual royalty from the first year, whatever the trial results show
A cross licence of the company's patents, so that no money changes hands at all
quiz.why: Royalties can be structured as a lump sum, a running royalty, an upfront fee with a running royalty, a minimum annual royalty, milestone payments, step-down rates, equity or a cross licence. Where success is uncertain and staged, milestone payments tie each payment to progress, and a running royalty shares the rewards once sales begin. A large lump sum or a high minimum royalty demands payment before results are known, which the licensee has refused, and a cross licence assumes the university wants the company's patents.

quiz.q: A patent changes hands for ₹5 crore, settled by issuing shares. An independent valuer had estimated its worth at ₹6 crore for that purpose and date, the seller's books carried it at ₹1 crore, and a bank said it would lend against ₹2 crore. Which description is correct?
quiz.ok: ₹6 crore is its value, ₹5 crore its price and ₹1 crore its carrying amount
no: ₹5 crore is its value, ₹6 crore its price and ₹2 crore its carrying amount
₹6 crore is its price, ₹5 crore its value and ₹1 crore its collateral value
₹1 crore is its value, ₹5 crore its price and ₹6 crore its collateral value
quiz.why: Value is an estimate of worth for a purpose and date, price is the amount actually agreed, consideration is what is actually given (here, shares), carrying amount is the figure in the accounts and collateral value is a lender's careful estimate of what it could recover on default. The ₹2 crore is therefore the collateral value. Keeping these apart stops a book figure or a deal price being mistaken for the asset's worth.

quiz.q: A patent has 14 years of legal term left, but the product it covers is expected to be overtaken by new technology in about 5 years. Over what period should a valuer project its income?
quiz.ok: About 5 years, its economic life, since income will stop before the legal term ends
no: 14 years, its legal life, since protection lasts for the full remaining term
Indefinitely, with a terminal value, since a good patent keeps earning income forever
Its useful life in the accounts, whatever the market and technology suggest
quiz.why: Legal life is the term of protection, economic life is the period during which the right earns income and is usually shorter, and useful life is the accounting estimate used for amortisation. New technology shortens economic life, so the income projection should stop when earnings stop. A patent with a fixed term should never be given a terminal value.

quiz.q: A songwriter's estate wants cash now from a stable stream of royalties, but it does not want to borrow or to give up ownership of the copyrights. Which route fits?
quiz.ok: Sell its future royalty stream to investors
no: A sale and licence back of the copyrights to investors
A loan secured by a charge over the copyrights
Venture debt secured on the song catalogue
quiz.why: The sale of future royalties to investors is a financing route of its own, separate from loans secured on IP, venture debt and sale and licence back. Selling the royalty stream raises cash from the income without borrowing and without transferring the copyrights. A sale and licence back gives up ownership, and the other two routes are borrowing.

quiz.q: A valuer must value a patent that faces a pending revocation petition with a real chance of success. Which approach handles this uncertainty as the notes suggest?
quiz.ok: Value scenarios with and without the patent surviving, and weight them by probability
no: Ignore the petition, since valuation assumes every granted patent is valid
Use the full legal life, since revocation has not yet been ordered by anyone
Add the expected litigation cost to the value, treating it as an investment in the patent
quiz.why: Valuers handle uncertainty through scenarios, sensitivity analysis, probability weighting, simulation and real options. A real risk of revocation would end the income stream early, so it must be reflected rather than ignored. Litigation cost reduces value; it is not an addition to it.

quiz.q: Commercialising a patent needs ₹30 crore now and is expected to bring ₹10, ₹12 and ₹14 crore at the end of years 1, 2 and 3. The discount rate is 10 per cent. What is the NPV, and should the firm go ahead?
quiz.ok: About −₹0.47 crore, so reject the project
no: About ₹6.00 crore, so accept the project
About ₹2.48 crore, so accept the project
About ₹29.53 crore, so accept the project
quiz.why: The present values are 10 ÷ 1.10 = 9.09, 12 ÷ 1.10² = 9.92 and 14 ÷ 1.10³ = 10.52, a total of 29.53, so NPV is 29.53 − 30 = −0.47 and the project should not proceed. ₹6.00 crore ignores discounting, ₹2.48 crore discounts each flow one year too little, and ₹29.53 crore forgets to deduct the initial investment. Discounting turns an apparently profitable project into a loss-making one.

quiz.q: Assume a risk-free rate of 6 per cent, a beta of 1.5, a market risk premium of 6 per cent, a capital structure of 70 per cent equity and 30 per cent debt, a pre-tax cost of debt of 12 per cent and a tax rate of 25 per cent. What is the WACC?
quiz.ok: 13.2 per cent
no: 14.1 per cent
10.8 per cent
9.0 per cent
quiz.why: The cost of equity is 6 + 1.5 × 6 = 15 per cent, the after-tax cost of debt is 12 × (1 − 0.25) = 9 per cent, and WACC is 0.7 × 15 + 0.3 × 9 = 13.2 per cent. 14.1 per cent forgets the tax saving on debt, 10.8 per cent swaps the weights, and 9.0 per cent leaves the risk-free rate out of the cost of equity. An extra premium for IP risks such as invalidity and obsolescence may then be added.

quiz.concept: Risk-adjusted NPV for a staged project
quiz.q: A drug candidate's trial costs ₹10 crore now (certain). A further ₹40 crore is spent at the end of year 1, a stage with a 50 per cent chance of being reached. Income of ₹200 crore arrives at the end of year 3, with a 20 per cent chance of being reached. At a 10 per cent discount rate, what is the risk-adjusted NPV?
quiz.ok: About ₹1.87 crore
no: About ₹103.90 crore
About ₹10.00 crore
About −₹16.31 crore
quiz.why: Each flow is multiplied by the chance of reaching it and then discounted: −10, −20 ÷ 1.10 = −18.18 and 40 ÷ 1.10³ = +30.05, giving about ₹1.87 crore. ₹103.90 crore ignores the probabilities and so is misleadingly high, ₹10.00 crore applies the probabilities but forgets to discount, and −₹16.31 crore weights only the income and not the year-1 cost. Legal facts such as remaining term and validity should fix the period and risk of the flows.

quiz.concept: Lump sum versus running royalty after tax
quiz.q: A licensor can take a lump sum of ₹4.4 crore now, or a 4 per cent running royalty on a licensee's sales of ₹50 crore a year for three years, received at each year end, less its own cost of ₹0.1 crore a year. Tax is 25 per cent on either, the discount rate is 10 per cent, and there is no doubt about the licensee's credit or the patent's validity. Which is better?
quiz.ok: The royalty, worth about ₹3.54 crore after tax against ₹3.30 crore for the lump sum
no: The lump sum, worth ₹4.40 crore against about ₹3.54 crore for the royalty after tax
The royalty, worth about ₹4.28 crore after tax against ₹3.30 crore for the lump sum
The royalty, worth about ₹4.73 crore before tax against ₹4.40 crore for the lump sum
quiz.why: Each year's royalty is 4 per cent × 50 = 2.0, less the 0.1 cost and 25 per cent tax, or 1.425; discounted at 10 per cent (1 ÷ 1.10 + 1 ÷ 1.10² + 1 ÷ 1.10³ = 2.4869) it is worth about ₹3.54 crore, against 4.4 × 0.75 = ₹3.30 crore for the lump sum after tax. Setting an after-tax royalty against an untaxed lump sum wrongly favours the lump sum, ₹4.28 crore forgets to discount, and ₹4.73 crore compares both before tax. Doubt about the licensee's credit or the patent's validity could reverse the choice.

quiz.q: A trade mark with no fixed end to its life is expected to earn ₹4 crore next year, with growth of 3 per cent a year after that. The discount rate is 11 per cent. What terminal value does the notes' formula give?
quiz.ok: About ₹50.00 crore
no: About ₹36.36 crore
About ₹51.50 crore
About ₹28.57 crore
quiz.why: Terminal value is next year's cash flow divided by (r − g): 4 ÷ (0.11 − 0.03) = ₹50.00 crore. ₹36.36 crore ignores growth, ₹51.50 crore grows next year's flow a second time, and ₹28.57 crore adds g to r instead of subtracting it. The formula suits an asset with no fixed end, such as this mark; a patent with a fixed term should not be given a terminal value.

quiz.concept: Reading IRR against the discount rate
quiz.q: A licence project has conventional cash flows (an outlay now, inflows later) and an IRR of 18 per cent. The firm's discount rate is 13 per cent. What follows?
quiz.ok: Its NPV at 13 per cent is positive, since it is discounted below the IRR
no: Its NPV at 13 per cent is negative, since the return falls short of the IRR
Its NPV at 13 per cent is zero, since IRR and NPV always give the same figure
Nothing about NPV follows, since IRR ignores the timing of the cash flows
quiz.why: The IRR is the discount rate at which NPV is zero. With an outlay followed by inflows, discounting at a rate below the IRR gives a positive NPV, so at 13 per cent the project is worthwhile. IRR is built from discounted flows, so it does take timing into account.

quiz.q: A licensee expects to earn a profit equal to 16 per cent of its sales of the licensed product. What royalty does the 25 per cent rule of thumb suggest?
quiz.ok: About 4 per cent of sales
no: About 12 per cent of sales
About 25 per cent of sales
About 16 per cent of sales
quiz.why: The rule gives the licensor about one quarter of the licensee's expected profit: 25 per cent × 16 per cent = 4 per cent of sales. 12 per cent gives the licensor three quarters instead of one quarter, 25 per cent applies the fraction to sales rather than profit, and 16 per cent hands over the whole profit. The rule is simple but widely criticised as arbitrary, so it needs a cross-check.

quiz.q: Five comparable licences show royalties of 2.0, 3.0, 4.5, 5.0 and 9.0 per cent. The four lower ones were non-exclusive licences of similar proven technology without support; the 9.0 per cent deal was exclusive and bundled know-how and on-site support. The licence being priced is exclusive, for proven technology, with no support. Which conclusion follows the notes' method?
quiz.ok: Median 4.5, middle range 3.0 to 5.0 per cent; price near its top, giving the 9.0 deal little weight
no: Simple average 4.7 per cent, since every comparable licence must be weighted equally
Price near 9.0 per cent, since the only exclusive comparable sets the right level
Median 4.5, middle range 3.0 to 5.0 per cent; price near its bottom, since no support is being given
quiz.why: Sorted, the five rates give a median of 4.5 per cent and a middle range of 3.0 to 5.0 per cent. Exclusivity justifies a point near the top of a range built from non-exclusive comparables, while the 9.0 per cent deal is less comparable because it bundled know-how and support. The absence of support explains why the price stays below that deal, not why it should fall to the bottom of the range.

quiz.q: In royalty benchmarking, an analyst finds a licence granted ten years ago, non-exclusive, in a different field of use and with technical support included. What should the analyst do with it?
quiz.ok: Adjust for the differences or give it little weight, then cross-check with income methods
no: Use its royalty unchanged, since any published licence counts as a valid comparable
Prefer it over recent deals, since an older licence has been better tested
